title: Changing chapter titles causes problems with serve_book
description:
Many thanks for this very useful resource. 

I encountered what seems to be a bug when using "serve_book". 

Suppose I have an Rmd file, say "an.Rmd", like the following 

```{r}
# Introsuction

Bloop.
```
When I serve the book, a file "introsuction.html" gets created in "_book".

If I edit "an.Rmd" in a way that changes the chapter title, such as 

```{r}
# Introduction

Bloop.

Bleep.
```
then a file "introduction.html" is created, but  "introsuction.html" is not deleted. 

This wouldn't be so bad, except the "index.html" file doesn't get rebuilt, and 
so  "introsuction.html" is served instead of "introduction.html."
Even when making further changes to "an.Rmd",  "introduction.html"  doesn't get 
served until index.html is rebuilt (e.g. if index.html gets changed).

title: gitbook feature request: arbitrarily exclude heading from TOC
description:
First I absolutely love the package and thanks so much for your hard work! My feature request is similar to how we can use `# H1 {-}` to prevent heading numbering. I would find it useful to have a syntax option within `{}` to arbitrarily exclude a particular header from the TOC. I have found myself choosing heading levels merely to get the TOC to display the way I want rather than reflecting the logical structure of the contents or how I want separate html pages to be built out. Consider the case where chapters have different levels of granularity. For instance, a "low resolution" vs "high resolution" set of chapters might look like:

```
# 1 Introduction (low res)
## 1.1 Section
## 1.2 Section
# 2 Chapter (high res)
## 2.1 Section
### 2.1.1 Subsection
### 2.1.2 Subsection
```
If I want my TOC to read:

- 1 Introduction
- 2 Chapter
  - 2.1 Section

Currently I could set `bookdown::gitbook:toc_depth: 2` in `_output.yml`. And rewrite my headings like this:

```
# 1 Introduction (low res)
### 1.1 Section
### 1.2 Section
# 2 Chapter (high res)
## 2.1 Section
### 2.1.1 Subsection
### 2.1.2 Subsection
```

But this is illogical and prevents 1.1 and 1.2 from being built as separate html pages. I imagined the solution could be something like this...

```
# 1 Introduction (low res)
## 1.1 Section {+}
## 1.2 Section {+}
# 2 Chapter (high res)
## 2.1 Section
### 2.1.1 Subsection
### 2.1.2 Subsection
```
...which could be a flag for ignoring those headings when building the TOC. In general, for long projects the TOC can get unwieldy fairly quickly, so manually paring it down is a feature I would really appreciate!

title: Feature request: arbitrary fonts and font sizes for the verbatim environment
description:
There are situations when a different monospaced font is used, in my situation I use Menlo because it has a more visually appealing tilde sign ~ compared to the default font, in a setup that produces a PDF file using xelatex.

But changing the font brought a host of new issues, some already solved, such as the font size (the default is too big, the \small is too small). There is also the issue of the space between the lines of the verbatim environment, depending on particular setups it might be too much space for the default font size.

Having described the situation, this is the fix I came across:

````
\usepackage{fancyvrb}
\usepackage{anyfontsize}
\DefineVerbatimEnvironment{verbatim}{Verbatim}{formatcom=%
{\linespread{0.9}\normalfont\ttfamily\fontsize{10}{12}\selectfont}}

\setmonofont{Menlo}
````

I can put this in the preamble but it would only affect the R output, while the R commands in the Highlighting environment would still be different. I thought it would be nice to have this feature globally offered with parameters in the .yml file: name of the font, the percentage (in this example 0.9) to shrink or enlarge the space between the lines, and perhaps the font size (only one parameter is needed, since 12 is simply obtained by multiplying 10 with 1.2).

One other thing which I had to solve, was related to the double quotes in the verbatim environment. As it turns out, this line:
````
\defaultfontfeatures{Ligatures=TeX,Scale=MatchLowercase}
````
caused the double quotes to appear like smart quotes (slightly inclined), apparently having something to do with the `Ligatures=TeX` part. Removing that (have no idea if it breaks something) seems to solve the double quotes issue as well.

Thanks,
Adrian

I have two problems with RStudio's integration with Bookdown (actually, make that three). Both of them are encoding related.

### 1. There is this perpetual error whenever I open my project in RStudio:

```
Error in yaml::yaml.load(string, ...) : 
  Scanner error: while scanning a simple key at line 3, column 1could not find expected ':' at line 4, column 1
```

I have no idea which yaml header is having problem. Here's `_bookdown.yml`, `_output.yml` and finally the little front matter from `index.Rmd`:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10719482/29102979-77f5c694-7cef-11e7-96e4-01ff0d0d9cb5.png)

Sorry I had to blot out the texts. Suffice it to say that they are all Chinese characters. This error seems to have no consequences. The project builds normally, and all texts are correctly encoded.

### 2. R code with Chinese characters in them, in standalone code blocks, are highlighted as `unexpected token` by RStudio. 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10719482/29103265-24cc819a-7cf1-11e7-908f-de9bef6b63f6.png)

This kind of code is usually not an issue in a normal `.R` file. Although from time to time RStudio would choke on some lines ending with Chinese characters, I think. But I digress. Again, the code runs fine, but it is hard to ignore those wavy red lines.

### 3. RStudio gets a bit choppy when there's more than a couple of `Rmd`'s in the project. 

I have 10 `Rmd`'s in my project, a few plots and tables and hardly a thousand words between them. Yet when I type something, it's like I'm in a bad SSH tunnel. Keystrokes takes a subtle half-second to appear. Absolutely touching my nerves. However other UI elements seems fine; even the console performs normally. Just the editor.

I do think this is related to the parser/loader thingy that is causing **1** and **2**. I realize that there might be no fix save for switching to a GNU system.

Sometimes it is hard to believe that after all these years Windows still can't provide a stable and predictable multilingual dev environment.

title: Markdown superscript notation problem in kable caption for `pdf_document2`
description:
Hi bookdown developers,

Today I observed a possible bug behavior regarding to the markdown notation in table captions. I tried to isolate the problem I found that `pdf_document` and `bookdown::pdf_document2` have different behavior for the caption argument in the `knitr::kable()` function. The code below uses the markdown notation `^.^` and `~.~` to write super and subscripts.

    ---
    title: "Testing kable"
    output: bookdown::pdf_document2
    ---

    The gravity on earth is 9.8 m s^-2^. The water molecule is H~2~O.

    ```{r, echo = FALSE}
    library(knitr)
    cap <- "A caption with markdown notation for superscript 10 m s^-1^."
    kable(head(iris), caption = cap)
    ```

But, when `bookdown::pdf_document2` is used (default for `pdf_book` that I'm authoring), something coerces the output beeing interpreted as is. With the `pdf_document`, there is no problem. Below is the produced LaTeX code when using the `keep_tex: true` option in the YAML.

```
\textbackslash{}begin\{table\}
\textbackslash{}caption\{\label{tab:unnamed-chunk-1}A caption with markdown
notation for superscript 10 m s\textsuperscript{-1}.\} \centering
... code omited ...
\textbackslash{}end\{table\}
```

The `^-1^` notation is interpreted correctly to LaTeX producing `\textsuperscript{-1}`. But the `\textbackslash{}` isn't expected to happen. This messed up the things below this table, mostly because the `\centering` command.

In advance, I appreciate your attention.
Thank you.

title: let render_book default to envir = new_env(), not parent.frame() to avoid side-effect-trap
description:
I recently spent a couple of hours figuratively shooting myself in the foot with `bookdown::render_book()` scoping shenanigans.
It was stupid, painful and unnecessary, and I'm wondering whether others might fall into the same trap and/or whether a different default could protect users like myself *from* themselves.

----

**Problem**

I was building a custom render function with some internal control logic. (I used some logical flags as arguments, say `docs = TRUE`, which would indicate whether I *also* wanted to, say, run `pkgdown::build_site()`).

So I had something like this:

```
render_book2 <- function(docs = TRUE) {
  bookdown::render_book(
    input = "index.Rmd",
    output_format = 'bookdown::gitbook',
    output_dir = '../../_site/book'
  )
  if (docs) {
    # `pkgdown::build_site()`. # my actual use case
    cat("docs is currently set to", docs)  # just for reprex purposes
  }
}
```

This function worked fine from the R console, but failed when run via `Rscript e ...` with an ominous `Object docs cannot be found` (not verbatim), which baffled me.

The reason, I realised after *way* too many more rounds is because `envir = parent.frame()` *and* `clean_envir = !interactive()` by default.
(The `clean_envir = !interactive()` bit explains the different behavior between R console and `Rscript e ...`.).

Once I had figured this out, the problem is clear: `bookdown::render_book()`, via `clean_envir = TRUE` removes all objects from the *parent* (?) environment, which here is the custom `render_book2()` function, so logical flags (such as `docs`) are gone by the time they're used in the control flow.

So, it's a **side effect** of `bookdown::render_book()` if used *with defaults*.

----

**Solution**

Once I figured this out, I fixed the problem by setting `envir = new.env()` as advised in the `rmarkdown::render_site()` docs.

----

**Comment**

I think I understand the `clean_envir = !(interactive)` default.
Actually I always want `clean_envir = TRUE` because it is a good idea to avoid potentially lingering objects from past builds to different formats.

But together with `envir = parent.frame()` this leads to an easy trap if used programmatically.

I wonder whether others might fall into this with the defaults too.


----

**Solution**

**Might `envir = new_env()` be a safer default for `render_book()`?**

Scoping and environments generally give me the shivers, so I might be missing something obvious here.

title: new_session is incompatible with RMDs in a subdirectory
description:
When `new_session` is set to `no` (by default), you can put RMD files in a subdirectory and include their relative path in `_bookdown.yml`. For example:

    new_session: no
    rmd_files: ["index.Rmd", "chapters/01-intro.Rmd", "chapters/02-literature.Rmd"]

However, if `new_session` is set to `yes`, the build will throw the following error:

    ==> rmarkdown::render_site(encoding = 'UTF-8')
    
    Error in render_book("index.Rmd", output_format = output_format, envir = envir) : 
      All input files must be under the current working directory
    Calls: <Anonymous> ... <Anonymous> -> in_dir -> render_book_script -> render_book
    Execution halted
    
    Exited with status 1.

Either putting the RMDs in the root directory or setting `new_session` to `no` makes the error go away.

Here is a fork of bookdown-demo with files in a subdirectory that you can test - https://github.com/steveharoz/bookdown-demo

title: hidden setting when specifying `template: default` in YAML
description:
See the discussion in the comments of this [stackoverflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44770287/adding-natbib-options-for-pdf-output)

Setting `template: default` in the bookdown YAML for LaTeX/PDF output does not have the same result as specifying the default template provided by rmarkdown (which is only apparent if you follow the `pdf_document` argument `base_format` to the source code of `rmarkdown::pdf_document`). It appears that `geometry: "margin=1in"` gets set internally when `template: default` is specified, but is not set when you specify the path to the default template file itself. This is confusing, and can lead people (like me!) astray when they start trying to customize a template and are unable to reproduce the default look of the pdf document. It would be good to remove this inconsistent behavior, or at least document this somewhere,.

On a more general note, I think it would be helpful for bookdown include the default LaTeX template with the package (as it does with the HTML templates), even if it is redundant. It would make it easier for users to access the default template and build off it, and would allow bookdown to provide its own default template in the future that might be more appropriate for books than the default pandoc template. Alternatively, an explicit statement of where to find the "default" template and would be helpful.

title: `render_book()` should not touch the source `.Rmd` files
description:
First thanks a lot for the fantastic work you're doing with **knitr** and **bookdown**!

I have the following concern: I have noticed that `bookdown::render_book()` touches the `.Rmd` source files. I'm using the knit-then-merge approach and I'm using a before-chapter script, just like Hadley does in his r4ds book. What appears to be happening is that the before-chapter script is actually inserted into the source `.Rmd` file, then the file is knitted, and then the original source file is restored. This problematic for at least two reasons:

1. Most importantly, I've had several instances when the before-chapter script was not properly removed from the source file. I'm not sure exactly when this happens, but it could be a race condition between `render_book()` and my editor, i.e., `render_book()` changes the file, my editor picks it up, then I modify the file in my editor before `render_book()` restores it, and I end up with a source file that contains the before-chapter script.

2. More generally, though, I don't think any compilation process should touch source files at all. It messes up time stamps, and it risks corruption of the original source if anything goes wrong, e.g. the compile crashes, the power goes out, whatever.

The correct approach would be to copy the source file into a temporary file, modify the temporary file, knit that, and then delete.

description:
As suggested in https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/a-single-document.html I use html_document2() to write reports with bookdown which provides cross reference features.

I also like to embed the Rmd and have code chunks,  to be be collapsible, so I use:

```yaml
  bookdown::html_document2:
    base_format: rmarkdown::html_notebook
    code_folding: hide
```

However, knitting to html_document2 saves the file using the ".nb.html" extension imported from html_notebook. Doing a regular File/Save within RStudio overwrites this file.

It would be nice to add an option to support a regular ".html" extension, so that the File/Save would only overwrite the source file.Rmd and the preview file.nb.html

title: Do not copy external CSS/Fonts when rendering?
description:
Another blunder by me, I suppose. 

If I set `output_dir` to `../_book`, and use a custom CSS with `css: ../styles/style.css`, then upon `render_site`, any and all files referenced by the custom CSS, along with the CSS itself, would be overwritten, and corrupt.

After:
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/10719482/26229229/f134ca90-3c72-11e7-902a-222ba5d2cf97.png)

Those two `NotoSerifCJK` fonts that weren't changed were not referenced in the CSS. As you could imagine, custom CSS won't work anymore.

I'd like to know if there is any way to disable this copying behaviour, and prefereably leave the stylesheet reference unchanged.

title: Protect users from their own stupidity?
description:
Alright I've done something very stupid. I'll spare you the confusion and panic, and get straight to the point.

title: Impossible to add numbered equations within a paragraph because Pandoc adds unwanted line breaks
description:
Pandoc adds extra line breaks around LaTeX environments such as `equation`, `align` and friends. In regular R Markdown this doesn't crop up too often as a problem, because we tend to use `\[ \]` or `$$ $$` instead. But in `pdf_book` and `pdf_document2` we can't use bookdown's equation numbering extension within paragraphs without vertical spacing and indentation issues.

For example, a single paragraph sequence like
```latex
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet,
\begin{equation}
E = mc^2,
\end{equation}
consectetur adipiscing elit.
```
is converted by pandoc into three paragraphs
```latex
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet,

\begin{equation}
E = mc^2,
\end{equation}

consectetur adipiscing elit.
```
which is not the same thing in LaTeX at all. It changes the vertical spacing completely (especially egregiously for `align` and `align*`) and, if `indent: true` is set, then indents the following sequence of text. Adding `\noindent` everywhere is not a solution, especially as it does nothing about the vertical spacing.

There is a [related issue](https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/issues/2171) on the pandoc repository.  Does anybody know any tricks to stop Pandoc from doing this, or else a way to remove the line breaks just before converting to PDF?

title: Internalization: changing word ordering
description:

I am working on a series of research reports, or rather books on an international research project that has to be produced in four or five Latin-character languages. Producing the English version is easy following the excellent authoring documentation. However, internalization appears to be painful, because there are virtually no examples (apart from non-Latin, Chinese) books, and the examples are not clear to me in the book. 

In a language where Chapter 1 would be like 1. fejezet, you would need to use this recommended approach:

>  R function that takes the chapter number as the input and returns a string as the new chapter number 
 >(e.g.,` !expr function(i) paste('Chapter', i)`). If it is a character vector of length 2, the chapter title prefix 
> will be `paste0(chapter_name[1], i, chapter_name[2])`, where i is the chapter number.

I assume that something like 
>` r paste0(i, ". fejezet")`  

should work (among the ' `...` ') code quotes, but I wonder how I can retrieve the chapter number and passed it to [`i`], and how can have the expression evaluated from the` _bookdown.yml `file.  It is unclear to me in the example how can I get
>` !expr function(i) paste('Chapter', i)`

executed (and why` !expr `? )

Furthermore, I wonder if this approach can be taken to other possible label elements, such as
> `tab: 'Table "`

if it should become 1.1. táblázat? 

A workaround to internalization would be relying on the .tex output created for `pdf_book()` but as I [reported earlier](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/issues/342), the .tex file cannot be compiled because it refers to temporary directory that I cannot retrieve.  I generally believe that with more and more languages tried in bookdown, there will be other issues unexpected from an English/Chinese background, and a first step could be tinkering the .tex file, and then possibly adding a bit more internalization features to bookdown.

title: Best practices for multiple columns?
description:
Folks over at the [Marshall Project](https://www.themarshallproject.org/) published an [excellent analysis](https://www.themarshallproject.org/2016/08/18/crime-in-context ) of US crime data. 

While the content is fascinating, I was also struck by their effective use of layout to present a data-rich argument. For example:

![marshall-proj-ss](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8197328/22797547/80a13276-eeb3-11e6-8d94-8e050ba0886f.PNG)

I started looking into multi-column formats for bookdown and found that the situation is a little complicated. It seems like the biggest issue is getting consistency across the different output formats that bookdown allows (e.g., gitbook, pdf, word doc, etc.). But more fundamentally, there doesn't seem to be a clear source of documentation for how users should implement a mutli-column layout in a bookdown document.

Let's say I was interested in publishing a gitbook document, should I use [css method](http://stackoverflow.com/a/31754601/5170276) or the [bootstrap method](http://stackoverflow.com/a/38995154/5170276)? Is there a way to configure the document so that the 2-column format would also work with a pdf output?

title: EPUB output cannot handle references across chapters
description:
If one tries to have a link from one chapter to another, the links in the resulting epub are broken (they can't be resolved by epub readers like iBooks or by Kindlegen, etc). ### Reproducible example index.Rmd: ``` --- title: "Test Book" output: bookdown::epub_book --- # Chapter One See Chapter \@ref(chapter-two) for more. # Chapter Two This is Chapter Two. ``` Built with `bookdown::render_book("index.Rmd")`. Here is the relevant part of the resulting `_main.epub/ch001.xhtml`: ```

1 Chapter One

See Chapter 2 for more.

``` This link is broken; it should be to `ch002.xhtml#chapter-two`, or the epub readers won't know to link across chapters. Note that (in my understanding) this can't be handled by pandoc options, since the link is already generated in `_main.utf8.md` as `See Chapter 2 for more.`. The links would have to be resolved by bookdown.

title: Caching behavior
description:
I've been using `bookdown` for a while now, and I have to say I'm really impressed by the work done! It provides me the perfect tools for my work. I am just slightly puzzled by how cache is handled. In my case, I like to turn `cache = TRUE` in `knitr::opts_chunk$set`, so that it makes work-in-progress easier: all you have to do is to `render` the book and you have the session ready for use with every objects at hand.

Except that what works with vanilla `knitr` does not seem to work with `bookdown::render`. If I `render` a book, all objects are indeed created (as a call to `ls()`) indicates, but they are only pointers to the last cache version computed (for instance, epub), and the way `bookdown::render` reorganizes folders when it's done makes it unable to recover objects. For instance, if I create an object `x` in a RMarkdown file, render the book, and try to call `x` in the R console, I get error messages such as:

    Error: cannot open file '<working directory>/bookdown_cache/epub3/unnamed-chunk-
    1_53b327261f8a149223b65aef1557669f.rdb': No such file or directory

Which makes sense given that the actual cached object is now in `_bookdown_files/bookdown_cache/epub3/`, i.e. now in the `_bookdown_files` subfolder.

So my question is: Is this intended behavior? Is the cache mechanism just intended for the book, and not for users? (if yes, may I suggest that it would be a great idea that users can use it too, as is available through `knitr`)

Bonus question: What is the purpose of having different cache folders for different book formats? Shouldn't it be a single cache for all outputs? I'm not sure I see the benefits of having three (this is a huge computing + size overhead, plus the possibility that the different caches are not synced… which would lead to different outputs for different book formats…)

title: Support for algorithms and nomenclature with numbering and list of algorithms/nomenclature
description:
I'm evaluating whether to write my thesis in latex or bookdown. My latex template has incorporated support for numbered algorithms <https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/LaTeX/Algorithms>, code listings <https://www.sharelatex.com/learn/Code_listing> and nomenclature <https://www.sharelatex.com/learn/Nomenclatures> with corresponding lists of nomenclature/algorithms/code listings in the preamble.

Is support for these environments already possible with current versions of bookdown or they still have yet to be implemented?

title: Query about adding further docx compatibility to bookdown/pandoc
description:
Hi there, 

I'm interested in the following features, mostly to improving compatibility with the docx outputs (I know, don't ask!). I think for all of these the question is whether this is something that needs changing in bookdown or pandoc?

1. I'd love for custom `block2` environments to relate to a new style in the word document so that I could adjust that style in a template (like I can adjust the custom environment in the latex output). 
2. Is there any cross-target way to provide in-line images (in the text) rather than as a Figure. I was using `\include_graphics()` for the LaTeX outputs but that only works in LaTeX obviously. I've now switched to using the R `include_graphics()` but I can't work out with that how to add inline images
3. I guess the cross-target equivalent of `\index{}` won't be coming anytime soon?

Other than these things I'm quite impressed at how good the docx output is. Much better-looking than if I converted the pdf after creating it. bookdown is quite a help in allowing me to output both formats from a single source

many thanks

title: pass on DT::datatable(caption =) argument, label datatables as tables
description:
I'm relying a lot on `DT::datatable()` tables, rather than `knitr::kable()` static ones.

Because `DT::datatable()` is an `htmlwidget`, I seem to be able to set a reference-able, numbered caption *only* by relying on the knitr chunk option `fig.cap =`. (I hope I got this right).
This makes sense for *most* of the `htmlwidgets`, many of which are plots, but, I'd say, *not* for `DT::datatable()`, which is actually a table.

Referencing/captioning it as a figure might be confusing for users.

I've tried several approaches to get a `DT::datatable()` to be properly labeled as a *table*  in `bookdown::gitbook()`, but without success.

```{r, dt-repro, fig.cap="This is the caption from the code chunk"}
library(DT)
DT::datatable(head(iris), caption = "Table: This is the caption from inside DT")
```

```{r, dt-repro2}
DT::datatable(head(iris), caption = "(\\#tab:dt-repro) Table: This is the caption from inside DT")
```

```{r, dt-repro3}
knitr::kable(head(iris), caption = "This is the caption from inside kable")
```

yield, respectively,

![captions](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/22214845/7a201d62-e199-11e6-9a5c-ee17a6ce8eb2.png)

I think it would be nice if I the caption set inside `DT::datatable()` could be passed on to `bookdown()` in the appropriate way.

Alternatively, and to remain open to more custom tables, I was wondering whether a chunk option `tab.cap=` inside knitr might make sense, to be treated analogously to `fig.cap = `.

Ps.: This might seem like a somewhat trivial issue (whether an actual table is called a *figure*), but this gets thornier in use cases where people use `DT::datatable()` for HTML-type outputs, and `knitr::kable()` for others. In that (my) scenario, the whole numbering and referencing diverges between the different outputs.

title: Chunck option "fig.fullwidth=TRUE" does not produce full-width figure
description:
First of all, thank you for creating and maintaining something amazing. 

In the bookdown book, It says to refer to the `tufte` package documentation for special chunk options related to the tufte style. after some googling, it seems that the chunck option "fig.fullwidth" is used to create full width fiigures that span both columns of the tufte style. 

When using "tufte_html_book" as output, chunk option "fig.fullwidth=TRUE" does not result in a full width figure.  what am I doing wrong? 

Simple example code below. 

    ---
    title: "A Book"
    author: "Frida Gomam"
    site: bookdown::bookdown_site
    documentclass: book
    output:
      bookdown::tufte_html_book
    ---

    # Testing figure placement

    Full width figure.

    ```{r fig.fullwidth=TRUE}
    x <- rnorm(1000)
    y <- rnorm(1000)
    
    par(mfrow=c(1,2))
    plot(x)
    plot(y)
    ```

    ```{r fig.margin = TRUE}
    plot(y)
    ```

title: support abstract in gitbook output

I don't think this would require/warrant any extra HTML/CSS.

It'd just be nice if the abstract from that field showed up perhaps as

```
# Abstract {-}

blah blah abstract from the field `abstract:` in the toplevel YAML.
```

Is this possible?
Or is there a simple way to access the toplevel YAML *from inside* the document, so I could "paste" it myself?

title: speed up bookdown/rmarkdown/knitr by parallel computing (probably just parallel compilation)
description:
I love how much faster `bookdown::gitbook()` is relative to LaTeX compilation, but it can still be quite slow, even with caching etc.
I'm on a multicore machine, but bookdown (and the rest of the toolchain) only appears to use one core.

So I was wondering whether parts of this could be paralelized.

Of course, parallelising is also an issue for just what people write *inside* the chunks, and that's not `bookdown`'s problem.
Also, I guess that computing several chunks *in parallel* is near impossible because of possibly mutual dependencies, and detecting these (though the `autodep` option does something like this, right?).

One thing I wondered might work was just to compile the different *output formats* in parallel (say, LaTeX and gitbook). Would that be feasible?

Other ideas of what could be parallelised?

title: Need `graphics` when using template TeX
description:
Hello developers,

I'm now using this amazing bookdown package. I really appreciate using it. Thank you for the great work.

I started customize LaTeX and I realized a possible bug. When I run using the same default template (pandoc output gives `--template /usr/lib/R/site-library/rmarkdown/rmd/latex/default-1.17.0.2.tex `) an error in LaTeX occurs. See below two `_output.yml` settings.
```
# (1) Default minimal setting: no errors.
bookdown::pdf_book

# (2) Using the same template but explicitly in _output.yml: Error!
bookdown::pdf_book:
  template: /usr/lib/R/site-library/rmarkdown/rmd/latex/default-1.17.0.2.tex
```

Below is the error that occurs.

```
# Error while latex compilation.by using setting (2) in _output.yml
! Undefined control sequence.
l.150 {\centering \includegraphics
                                  [width=0.8\linewidth]{bookdown-demo_files/...
```

I started debug and I found difference in the pandoc call. Se bellow the pandoc call with the two `_output.yml` settings.

```
# Call using default _output.yml (2)
/usr/local/bin/pandoc +RTS -K512m -RTS bookdown-demo.utf8.md --to latex 
--from markdown+autolink_bare_uris+ascii_identifiers+tex_math_single_backslash 
--output bookdown-demo.tex --table-of-contents --toc-depth 2 --template 
/usr/lib/R/site-library/rmarkdown/rmd/latex/default-1.17.0.2.tex 
--number-sections --highlight-style haddock --latex-engine pdflatex 
--natbib --include-in-header config/preamble.tex --include-before-body 
config/before_body.tex --variable graphics=yes --variable 
'geometry:margin=1in' --variable tables=yes --standalone --bibliography 
book.bib --bibliography packages.bib

# _output.yml (2)
/usr/local/bin/pandoc +RTS -K512m -RTS bookdown-demo.utf8.md --to latex 
--from markdown+autolink_bare_uris+ascii_identifiers+tex_math_single_backslash 
--output bookdown-demo.tex --table-of-contents --toc-depth 2 --template 
/usr/lib/R/site-library/rmarkdown/rmd/latex/default-1.17.0.2.tex 
--number-sections --highlight-style haddock --latex-engine pdflatex 
--natbib --include-in-header config/preamble.tex --include-before-body 
config/before_body.tex --variable tables=yes --standalone 
--bibliography book.bib --bibliography packages.bib
```

The difference is only these two variables: `--variable graphics=yes --variable 
'geometry:margin=1in'` that the latter (2) doesn't define. So I defined them in the `index.Rmd` YAML and it worked. Se below my `index.Rmd` header YAML.
```
---
title: "Planejamento e Análise de Experimentos"
author: "Prof. Walmes M. Zeviani"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), format = '%d de %B de %Y')`"
description: "Meu primeiro bookdown."
# --- LaTeX ----
graphics: yes
geometry: 'margin=1in'
documentclass: book
bibliography: [book.bib, packages.bib]
biblio-style: apalike
link-citations: yes
---
```

Is this a bug or a known case?

Thanks.

title: Extra files generated from within knitr::knit_print
description:
I'm developing a pacakge 'widgetframe' https://github.com/bhaskarvk/widgetframe, which allows you to wrap a widget inside an iframe. This could come really handy for bookdown to make sure that the book's CSS/JS don't interfere with the widget's CSS/JS. The basic idea is very simple, If you have something like below in your R markdown say 'example01.Rmd'... 
```{r w01}
widgetframe::frameWidget(leaflet::leaflet()))
```
Then when you knit this markdown it will result in two files, example01.html and widgets_w01.html. The example01.html will contain an iframe whose src attribute is 'widget_w01.html' and widgets_w01.html will contain the leaflet widget. This way the widget is displayed inside an iFrame and thus unaffected by the style used by the Rmd. This works very well for a stand alone Rmd file, but in case of bookdown, the `widgets_w01.html` is not moved to the book dir (_book by default). Is is possible to move all generated HTML artifacts from a knitting operation? Or alternatively is there a way to somehow override bookdown's behavior in my package so that I can move the widget HTML files when the book is rendered?

title: Theorem environments do not appear when echo = FALSE
description:
It took me a little while to figure this out, but it appears that environments such as theorems, proofs and so on are silently hidden if the default chunk option is `echo = FALSE`.

That is to say, if we have
```r
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
```
somewhere at the start of the document, then an environment
``````
```{theorem}
To be, or not to be, that is the question
```
``````
will not appear in the output. The solution in this case is to put
``````
```{theorem, echo = TRUE}
Is it nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune... (etc)
```
``````
and then the theorem will appear.

I'm not suggesting this is necessarily a *bug*, but it should probably be documented, as this behaviour isn't obvious. Just in case anybody else runs into the same problem.

title: Figure numbers in PDF-output with parts can be wrong
description:
Sometimes it is convenient to put some text after a (PART) title, and before the chapter title:

```
(PART) Title of second part

Here comes a little bit explanation on the part itself. And sometimes, with a figure.

![Figure caption](filename.png)

# Title of my fourth chapter in the book
```

When a figure is inserted in that piece of text, HTML output will reference it as figure **II.1** in the above example, which is convenient. However, PDF output uses the number of the _previous_ chapter as the prefix; **3.x** in this example (x being the xth figure from chapter 3). This would better be avoided; the HTML approach seems most logical.

I attached an [RStudio project](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/files/621299/bookdowntest.zip) to reproduce this (zip file, also containing pdf and tex in the _book folder).

title: Some things that go wrong with parts in pdf_document2
description:
I experience issues with _parts_ in pdf output formats (pdf_document2, and the same holds for pdf_book), similar to those in issue #221. I have attached a copy ([zipfile](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/files/595478/issue_parts_pdf.zip)) of this small RStudio project so that you can reproduce it, and the resulting [pdf-document](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/files/595477/_main.pdf) as well. I attached the TeX-file in another [zipfile](https://github.com/rstudio/bookdown/files/595483/texfile.zip).

Also, see the screenshot below.

Note that I have made a cross-reference in the last chapter to _'my first part'_, using [pandoc markdown's auto-identifiers](http://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#header-identifiers) as I couldn't get this to work with bookdown's cross-referencing style.

What goes wrong is this:

- **'(PART) ...'** appears in the table of contents for both parts. This happens irrespective of cross-referencing to parts or not.
- for parts which are **cross-referenced** in markdown:
    - the page with the numbered part title disappears, and an unnumbered chapter '(PART) ...' is added on a separate page.
    - the numbered part title disappears from the table of contents, while the '(PART) ...' line does not.
    - the numbering of parts does not take into account these parts.
- the **hierarchy** of parts and chapters in the pdf-file is broken when making cross-references to parts (_left side of the screenshot_). The following can happen (only partly visible in the attached case): when a part is inserted that is not cross-referenced (and therefore correctly distinguished), all subsequent _chapters plus cross-referenced parts_ are at the same level, below the level of the not-cross-referenced part.

In the meantime I manage to fix these things in TeX, but of course that is a manual step that does not survive new runs (and I also maintain HTML output from the same Rmd project).

title: Reference and caption code chunk
description:
I'm interested in being able to reference code listings alongside a caption in a manner similar to figures. For example, if I had a code chunk called `dobootstrap` 

It might look like so:

````
```{r dobootstrap, code.cap = "Illustrates the overall procedure for writing a simple random sample with replacement bootstrap."}
bootstrap = function(xt, B = 100, func = mean, ...) {
  results = rep(NA, B)   # Storage Vector
  n = length(xt)             # Length of Data
  
  for (i in seq_len(B)) {   # Begin Bootstrap
    xt_star  = xt[sample(n, n, replace = T)] # Generate new data
  results[i] = func(xt_star, ...) # Obtain statistic
  }
  
  results                         # Return bootstrapped test distribution
}
```
````

Then the reference would be `\@ref(code:dobootstrap)`.

Presently, the only way to reference a chunk seems to be to have it generate a figure and apply a caption with `fig.cap`.

             if (x == 0) return(0); 
             if (x == 1) return(1);

title: Add inter-.rmd hierarchy for nested depth
description:
Caveats - I'm not an R programmer, and this is just my novice opinion.  This is an enhancement request.

I was excited to adopt Bookdown until I ran into a dealbreaker - lack of inter-file hierarchical nesting.  

Bookdown allows ToC hierarchical nesting, but in the file system all .rmd files are equals.  Hierarchy is expressed intra-.rmd.  

This places a practical ceiling on depth of nesting and total length of the book.  Past a certain length, outline folding and navigation within a single .rmd file become unwieldy.  

Here is my design suggestion: 
1.  Make the default directory for .rmd or .md files a directory like /markdown instead of the root.  This improves ergonomics.
2.  Permit subfolder nesting.  Subfolders denote nesting hierarchy.  Each subfolder may have its own index.rmd file.  If it does not have one, then the heading is simply a placeholder which prints an index of the subfolder's contents.

Benefits: 

This allows a much more fluid book-writing workflow.  The author can start with a single .rmd.  When it gets long, he splits it in two.  Ibid... When he has 15 .rmd's, he begins nesting them into subfolders.  Throughout all these many structural edits, he doesn't need to touch any config files.  He can just alter the numerical prefixes of the files and folders to change their order in the ToC. 

Thus an author may concentrate on writing and let the content organically dictate the structure of his book.

Now, with leaden heart, I will plod into the cold wilderness of Docbook...

You can find a minimal `index.Rmd` file here [https://github.com/tinu-schneider/bookdown-figures-example](https://github.com/tinu-schneider/bookdown-figures-example) ### Example one The chunk option takes only a name, like `{r example-1}` and we plot a simple plot with `plot(1:10)` Then the plot in the `.tex` file has - no floating `figure` environment, it is added directly into the text - the file type `.pdf` added to the filename ``` r \includegraphics{.../figure-latex/example-1-1.pdf} ``` ### Example two Chunk options `{r example-2, fig.cap='A simple figure, example 2'}` Details in the `.tex` file - file type `.pdf` added to the filename - `\label` sits inside the `\caption{}` - figure is centered with `\centering` ``` r \begin{figure}[htbp] \centering \includegraphics{.../figure-latex/example-2-1.pdf} \caption{\label{fig:example-2}A simple figure, example 2} \end{figure} ``` ### Further examples Chunk options `{r example-3, fig.cap='Example 3', out.width='80%'}` `{r example-4, fig.cap='Example 4', out.width='80%', fig.asp=0.75}` `{r example-5, fig.cap='Example 5', out.width='80%', fig.asp=0.75, fig.align='center'}` Details in the `.tex` file - Positioning options to `figure` environment is missing (no `[htbp]`) - No file type added (which is ok) - `\centering` is added only when explicitly declared it in the options (which is ok)
All in all the plots are generated and included in the generated `book` more or less how I expect them to appear (no clear bug). But I don't understand the different behaviour when the `.tex` file is generated. I work on Win10 with MixTex and RStudio.

```{r nice-fig, fig.cap='Here is a nice figure!', out.width='80%', fig.asp=.75,     fig.align='center'}

Reference a figure by its code chunk label with the `fig:` prefix, e.g., see     Figure \@ref(fig:nice-fig). Similarly, you can reference tables generated from     `knitr::kable()`, e.g., see Table \@ref(tab:nice-tab).

```{r nice-tab, tidy=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  head(iris, 20), caption = 'Here is a nice table!',

)
```

# Test 2

```{r nice-fig2, fig.cap='Here is a nice figure!', out.width='80%',   fig.asp=.75,   fig.align='center'}
par(mar = c(4, 4, .1, .1))
plot(pressure, type = 'b', pch = 19)
```

Reference a figure by its code chunk label with the `fig:` prefix, e.g., see     Figure \@ref(fig:nice-fig2). Similarly, you can reference tables generated from     `knitr::kable()`, e.g., see Table \@ref(tab:nice-tab2).

```{r nice-tab2, tidy=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  head(iris, 20), caption = 'Here is a nice table!',
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```
``````

While the first two cross-references work as expected, the second paragraph renders as,

> Reference a figure by its code chunk label with the fig: prefix, e.g., see Figure **3**. Similarly, you can reference tables generated from knitr::kable(), e.g., see Table 2.

It should be Figure 2. And the captions are

![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 20 22 57](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17839046/1a1c3f08-67dd-11e6-878e-7b2715a56c93.png)

It does _not_ work with `bookdown::tufte_handout2()`:

![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 20 24 09](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17839052/3d45e722-67dd-11e6-86e0-7f3d27ae99b1.png)

Astonishingly, it works fine with `bookdown::pdf_book()`, which is _also_ LaTeX:

![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 20 25 50](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17839067/7c19bbc2-67dd-11e6-9c75-36a50f3de3c6.png)

_Even weirder_, when looking at the retained `*.tex` produced by `bookdown::tufte_handout2()`, the tex looks just fine:

```
...
blah blah in table \ref{tab:desc-example}) blah
...
\caption{\label{tab:desc-example}Description Matrix (Subset)}
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{r|l}
\hline
Index & Description\\
\hline
1 & animals\\
\hline
7 & pronounciation\\
\hline
8 & punctuation\\
\hline
12 & rhymes\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

Sure enough, when compiling the tex again from the _tex_ source, I get:

![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 20 28 44](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17839086/e7d7ce12-67dd-11e6-84f9-1ccb30d943f1.png)

(though, naturally, the intermediate `*.tex` doesn't work well, because it can't find other stuff as it should, being in a different directory).

---

This problem ... feels ... familiar from working directly in LaTeX ... feels like it wasn't run often enough ... .

**Hypothesis: `bookdown::tufte_handout2()` somehow doesn't run LaTeX often enough for table crossrefs to resolve. `bookdown::pdf_book()` _does_ run LaTeX often enough.**.

title: several include_graphics calls behave differently than several qplot calls
description:
Consider these three examples:

**Chunk with margin.fig = TRUE and 4 qplots and vector of 4 fig.cap**

``` r q-pic, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap=c("Participant considers all items.", "Participant chooses two *similar* items, names category.", "Participant applies categories to all items.", "All items are categorized as TRUE or FALSE."), dpi = 72, fig.margin = TRUE, fig.show = "asis"
qplot(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
qplot(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
qplot(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
qplot(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
```

yields **as intended, with different captions**
![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 13 52 11](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17836975/ab942e6e-67a6-11e6-95f9-1adccb017442.png)

---

**Chunk with margin.fig = TRUE and 4 include_graphics and vector of 4 fig.cap**

``` r q-pic, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap=c("Participant considers all items.", "Participant chooses two *similar* items, names category.", "Participant applies categories to all items.", "All items are categorized as TRUE or FALSE."), dpi = 72, fig.margin = TRUE, fig.show = "asis"
include_graphics(path = "img/q-cat-stage-0.png")
include_graphics(path = "img/q-cat-stage-1.png")
include_graphics(path = "img/q-cat-stage-2.png")
include_graphics(path = "img/q-cat-stage-3.png")
```

yields **incorrectly with all the same captions**
![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 13 52 55](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17836980/cd2f26aa-67a6-11e6-89d0-79bf5f6e7e4d.png)

---

**Chunk with margin.fig = TRUE and include_graphics() with 4-long vector and vector of 4 fig.cap**

lastly, when passing a vector to `include_graphics()`, it **works fine again**

``` r q-pic, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap=c("Participant considers all items.", "Participant chooses two *similar* items, names category.", "Participant applies categories to all items.", "All items are categorized as TRUE or FALSE."), dpi = 72, fig.margin = TRUE, fig.show = "asis"
include_graphics(path = c("img/q-cat-stage-0.png", "img/q-cat-stage-1.png", "img/q-cat-stage-2.png", "img/q-cat-stage-3.png"))
```

![screen shot 2016-08-21 at 13 55 36](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/17837003/4d52203a-67a7-11e6-86a7-22bb56f41da6.png)

---

I expected that `include_graphics()` would behave basically like any other graphics-producing call, but that appears not to be the case; to set _separate_ `fig.cap` for each plot, the `include_graphics()` must called _only_ once, with a vector of files.
`qplot()` can be called several times, and uses the different `fig.cap` as intended.

Is this intended behavior, or did I miss something?

> Error in parse_block(g[-1], g[1], params.src) : duplicate label 'intro_load'

---

bibliography: [book.bib]

title: [FR] Specify encoding  for render_site via bookdown_site generator
First chapter in a part comes and goes in preview
description:
I'm using the `(PART)` token as described here: https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/markdown-syntax.html.

If I use RStudio's Build Book, the sidebar appears as I expect.

But if I edit then update a single chapter and update the preview by knitting just that chapter, via "Knit", the first chapter in each part disappears from the sidebar. This even affects chapter numbering. I can still navigate to those pages via arrows and, after various amounts of internal navigation, the first chapters reappear in the sidebar and the chapters get renumbered.

title: Cross-reference with custom link text?
description:
I am successfully cross-referencing with `\@ref(label)` as described here:

https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/cross-references.html

But this forces me to write "chapter `\@ref(label)`".

Is there a way to create links in a more conventional markdown style where I get to write the text?

In http://r4ds.had.co.nz @hadley uses simple square brackets to achieve this, e.g. `[functions]` to link to the functions chapter. But damn if I can figure out why this works. It does not work for me.

title: Deletion of several .md chapters!
description: I just decided to experiment with the `(PART)` token. When I first tried to save this file, I got an unexpected message. It was so weird I took a screenshot, just in case ... I clicked No. File stayed open. Next attempt to save worked. BUT all my other chapters were deleted. Check out my Git pane: Luckily I committed just prior to this experiment, so have lost nothing. But others might not be so lucky. I feel like I experienced intermittent single file disappearance earlier, but nothing I could really describe clearly enough to merit an issue. This is a big one though. Any idea what just happened?

title: possible to preview README.md?
description: If I am editing `README.md` and use the keyboard shortcut for "knit" or click "Preview", I am taken to a preview of my book, pointed at index.html. I was only able to preview my README via `rmarkdown::render("README.md")` + open the html in the browser. Am I missing something? Or could `README.md` be treated in a more conventional way in the bookdown context?

title: How to deploy without publicizing?
description: I am embarrassed to see an experiment of ours (@daattali's version/fork) showing up on https://bookdown.org. This has no content. ~~BTW I've got him working to bring that down!~~ _at least it 404s now_ How can one develop a book, up to and including deployment, but NOT have it show up somewhere like that? I don't want to leave deployment to the end, because I've learned from, e.g., Shiny, that only leads to heartache. And I don't mind the development version being visible to someone who knows a URL or bothers to look on GitHub. But how can I keep it from appearing on https://bookdown.org as if I want people to read it?

title: Suggestion: add example book that shows how to publish with on GitHub
description:
I'm playing around with bookdown and it's awesome. @jennybc and I want to use it and have it ready for the upcoming useR. 

I just read the section on [publishing with GitHub](https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/github.html) and I'm a bit confused and not exactly sure how it works. It would be very helpful IMO if there was an example github repository that was set up to serve a bookdown book so that we can see how everything should look.

The part I'm mostly confused about is that currently the entire book project is a repository: [link](https://github.com/daattali/happy-git-with-r).  But the actual book HTML is inside the `_book`. folder, so in order to actually access the book, I need to go to daattali.github.io/happy-git-with-r/_book 

Can we have one repo that contains both the book metadata and source and HTML output?  I also wasn't sure if the `.nojekyll` file should go in the root dir or in the `_book` dir.

I hope these questions make sense!

title: Suggestion: use pandoc-crossref filter
description:
For referencing equations and figures, there's a pandoc filter called [pandoc-crossref](https://github.com/lierdakil/pandoc-crossref), which has very nice syntax. For example, equations are labelled directly: 
$$ \pi = 3 $$ #{eq:pi}
That's less cumbersome than the current approach (for equations at least). 
Since pandoc-citeproc is already used, perhaps crossref could be included as well?

title: latex macros not working in \equation{} environment
description:
pandoc supports directly defining Latex macros directly in the markdown, e.g.
\newcommand{\a}{\mathcal{alpha}}
This works fine in bookdown, as long as one uses the $$ syntax, but not when using the \equation syntax, meaning it's not possible to have a numbered equation with a macro in it. The reason as far as I can tell is that pandoc expands the macros directly when outputting html, but only when the math appears between $$. 
I guess a possible workaround is to also copy all the macros into an html preamble, but it is cumbersome. It would be great to have a unified mechanism.

title: adding a glossary

If it is possible to implement, here's my approach in case you have any suggestions.

Added to `preamble.tex`:

```
\usepackage[nomain,acronym,xindy,toc]{glossaries}
\makeglossaries
\usepackage[xindy]{imakeidx}
\makeindex
\input{glossary}
```

`glossary.tex` contains glossary entries, such as:

```
\newglossaryentry{computer}
{
  name=computer,
  description={is a programmable machine that receives input,
               stores and manipulates data, and provides
               output in a useful format}
}
```

In the rmd files I use `\gls{computer}`, ending with:

```
\printindex
\printglossaries
```

Ideally, these final commands would come after `\bibliography{}`, but I'm not sure how.

title: Title Documents

title: Cross-Reference Section by Title
description:
Currently, I can use `@\ref{}` to add a reference to a section, which will insert the numerical ID of the section. I'd prefer, in some cases, to have the link contain the section title (which may, of course, be different from the bookmark title). e.g.

```
You'll find more information in the '@\ref(somesect)' section.

## Something Here {#somesect}
```

My hope is that that would render as:

```
You'll find more information in the 'Something Here' section.
```

Maybe that requires an extra argument a la `@\ref(somesect, title=TRUE)`. Even if I had to manually provide the text for the link, that would be a feasible work-around for now.

title: Set output directory
description:
We run the following to compile HTML and PDF outputs

``` bash
R -e "setwd('/data');" \
   -e "bookdown::render_book('', bookdown::html_chapters(lib_dir='out/assets'), output_dir='out');"
   -e "bookdown::render_book('', 'bookdown::pdf_book', output_file='out/_main.pdf', output_dir='out')"
```

the hope is that all output files would be rendered in `./out`. It took some finagling to get that to work for both HTML and PDF, but it seems like the above set of options successfully executes. The issue is that the chapters HTML is still in the current directory, along with a slew of _main\* files. 

It would be great to have a way to avoid polluting the source tree and instead keep all rendered docs in a separate dir.

title: Allow duplicate chunk labels?
description: After merging all Rmd files, there might be duplicate chunk labels (e.g. the current ggplot2 book has this problem), we can allow such labels by setting a knitr option, but it may make the automatic figure/table labels unpredictable, e.g. a chunk with label `foo` may get `\label{fig:foo-1}` when the label is duplicated and knitr has automatically "corrected" it.
